stimulus.text:
“There is no Declaration of Rights; and the Laws of the general Government being paramount to the Laws & Constitution of the several States, the Declarations of Rights in the separate States are no Security. . . . In the House of Representatives there is not the Substance, but the Shadow only of Representation; which can never produce proper Information in the Legislature, or inspire Confidence in the people. . . . The Judiciary of the United States is so constructed & extended, as to absorb & destroy the Judiciarys of the several States. . . . There is no Declaration of any kind for preserving the Liberty of the Press, the Tryal by jury in civil Causes; nor against the Danger of standing Armies in time of Peace.”

—George Mason, Objections to the Constitution of Government formed by the Convention, September 1787

books.section: Topic 3.8 The Constitutional Convention and Debates over Ratification, C. Federalists, Anti-Federalists, and the Adoption of the Bill of Rights

primary_sources: George Mason, Objections to the Constitution of Government formed by the Convention (September 1787)

stem: Mason wrote these objections in September 1787 to do which of the following?

options.text: Defend the Constitution against its Anti-Federalist critics
options.misconception: Mason is one of the critics; the passage lists the Constitution's defects, not a defense of it.

options.text: Persuade others that the Constitution should not be adopted without protections for rights
Record the debates of the Convention for later historians
options.misconception: Mason wrote a list of objections to circulate, not a record of the debates; Madison's notes are that record.

options.text: Call for a second convention to write a bill of rights at once
options.misconception: Mason wanted protections added, but the passage calls for no second convention; it lists objections to the finished document.

rationales.B: Mason listed the Constitution's defects, above all the missing declaration of rights, to persuade others against adopting it as written. Background: he was one of three delegates who refused to sign, and his objections became the template for Anti-Federalist opposition.
rationales.A: The passage attacks the Constitution, so it cannot be a defense of it.
rationales.C: Mason circulated objections to persuade, not a record of the debates. Background: Madison's notes are that record.
rationales.D: The passage lists objections; it does not call for a second convention.
rationales.general:
1. The document is a list of objections to the finished Constitution.
2. Its first objection is the missing declaration of rights, and the rest follow the same pattern.
3. Background: Mason was one of three delegates who refused to sign in September 1787.
4. A list of objections written at that moment is an argument against adopting the document as written.
Remember: a list of defects is an argument against, so name the side it serves.
